summary: This standards-track document describes a GMPLS RSVP-TE mechanism that lets the network assign the upstream label of a bidirectional Label Switched Path. This is useful where a node cannot choose the label itself. The mechanism handles that case in the signaling.

eli5.summary: Two kids talk through a pipe and need to agree on which end is which. Here the network picks the end label for one direction instead of the kid doing it.

questions: how can the network assign an upstream label in gmpls
what is a bidirectional lsp upstream label
what is an unassigned upstream label
how does gmpls choose a wavelength for a bidirectional lsp
subtitle: A special all-ones label lets a GMPLS node ask the next node downstream to pick the upstream label for it.

tldr.problem: When setting up a bidirectional path, each upstream node must pick the upstream label itself, but sometimes it lacks the information to choose correctly, for example a router that cannot see which wavelength the optical network needs.
tldr.mechanism: The upstream node sends a Path message whose UPSTREAM_LABEL holds the special all-ones value (0xFFFFFFFF for a 4-octet label). The downstream node picks a symmetric label and returns it in the LABEL object of the Resv message.
tldr.outcome: The network, not the edge node, chooses the label, and can change it later. The RFC updates RFC 3471, RFC 3473 and RFC 6205 to allow this special label value.

today: RFC 8359 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, and it updates RFC 3471, RFC 3473 and RFC 6205.

sections.title: The Problem with Self-Chosen Labels
sections.content:
A bidirectional Label Switched Path (LSP) in GMPLS is set up with RSVP-TE. It is indicated by an UPSTREAM_LABEL object in the Path message. Under the existing procedure in RFC 3471 and RFC 3473, each upstream node must allocate a valid upstream label on its outgoing interface before it sends the first Path message downstream.

In some scenarios it is not desirable or possible for a node to pick that label on its own. This RFC defines a mechanism that lets the node hand the job to nodes downstream. It is meant only for bidirectional LSPs that use symmetric labels at each hop, such as Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) LSPs, which use symmetric lambda labels as in RFC 6205.
sections.eli5: Normally the sender must choose the channel before it starts talking. Sometimes the sender simply does not know which channel is safe, so it needs help.

sections.title: The Unassigned Upstream Label
sections.content:
The RFC defines a special label value, 0xFFFFFFFF for a 4-octet label, called the Unassigned Upstream Label. Similar all-ones patterns are expected for labels of other sizes.

When this value appears in the UPSTREAM_LABEL object of a Path message, it means the upstream node has not assigned an upstream label and asks the downstream node for a label usable in both the forward and reverse directions. The receiving node MUST also read it as a request to mandate symmetric labels for the LSP.

This changes two earlier rules. The UPSTREAM_LABEL may now carry a label that is not valid for forwarding, and in the LSC case it may differ from the value in the LABEL_SET object, which RFC 6205 required to be the same.
sections.eli5: A secret code, all ones, means 'I have not picked yet, please pick for both of us'. It is not a real channel.

sections.title: Signaling Procedures
sections.content:
The procedures cover only the exchange between an upstream node and its immediate downstream node. The upstream node sends a Path message with the Unassigned Upstream Label. If it wants to tell the downstream node about its limits, it MUST list the valid labels in a LABEL_SET object.

The downstream node picks a symmetric label and returns it in the LABEL object of the Resv message, and the upstream node then uses it in both directions. If the downstream node cannot pick one, it MUST send a PathErr message with a 'Routing Problem/Unacceptable Label Value' indication. If the upstream node gets back an all-ones label or any other unacceptable label, it MUST send a ResvErr with the same indication.

The upstream node keeps signaling the Unassigned Upstream Label even after it receives a label. This lets the downstream node choose a different symmetric label later. An unacceptable changed label again triggers a ResvErr.
sections.eli5: You ask, your friend answers with a channel, and you both use it. If your friend cannot find one, or gives you a bad one, someone says 'that will not work'.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
A downstream node that does not understand the new meaning will do one of two things. It may reject the special value with an error as in Section 3.1 of RFC 3473, in which case there is no compatibility concern.

Or it may accept the value as if it were a valid label. Then it will send an all-ones label in the LABEL object of the Resv message, and the upstream node answers with a ResvErr carrying 'Routing Problem/Unacceptable Label Value'.
sections.eli5: If your friend does not know the 'you choose' game, either they say so, or they answer with the secret code. Then you tell them it is not a real answer.

sections.title: Use Case: Wavelength Setup over Optical Networks
sections.content:
Routers A and B are clients of an optical WDM network, with WDM nodes F and I between them. A router's transponder is wired to an add-drop port on a WDM node. Depending on how multiplexing is implemented, a router sending the wrong wavelength may harm existing optical trails, and a client without full view of the optical network cannot pick the right one in advance.

In the initial setup, Router A sends a Path message with the Unassigned Upstream Label, and its laser stays off because the wavelength is unknown. Node F chooses the wavelength and forwards it in the label fields toward Router B. Router B turns its laser on and tunes it to that wavelength, then sends a Resv upstream. Router A receives a valid symmetric label in the LABEL object and then tunes and turns on its own laser.

Later, the network may change the wavelength for reasons such as policy, restoration within the core or preemption. Each client then retunes its laser when it receives the changed label in a modified Resv or Path message. Where the egress relies on signaling to know when to start using the LSP, the sequence can be combined with the ResvConf procedure of RFC 2205 or the two-step ADMIN STATUS procedure of RFC 3473.
sections.eli5: A router is like a flashlight that must be set to the right color before turning on. It waits, the network tells it the color, then it switches on. If the network later changes the color, it retunes.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA added a new subregistry, 'Special Purpose Generalized Label Values', to the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry. New values are assigned by Standards Action. The first entry is the all-ones pattern, named Unassigned Upstream Label, applicable to UPSTREAM_LABEL.

On security, the RFC says the change only affects the meaning of one field in an existing RSVP object, so it raises no new security implications and the considerations in RFC 3473 still apply. It points to RFC 5920 for general MPLS and GMPLS security.
sections.eli5: The special code is written in an official list so nobody uses it for something else. It adds no new dangers.
